name: Steelmouth
description:
Hamilton was built on steel, and steel is still what Hamilton tastes like. The foundries that lined Burlington Bay in the twentieth century have been replaced by advanced metallurgical facilities producing augmentation-grade alloys, structural composites for arcology construction, and military-specification armor plating. Palladian Construction and Ashgrave Materials maintain sovereign manufacturing zones along the waterfront, their territory extending from the bay shore to the escarpment face — a vertical boundary that divides the city as cleanly as any corporate jurisdiction line. Below the escarpment: industry, smoke, and the people who make things. Above: residential towers for the managers, the engineers, and the people who profit from what gets made below.

The escarpment itself — a 100-meter limestone cliff running east-west through the city — is Steelmouth's defining geographic feature and its most literal class boundary. Elevators and cargo lifts connect the upper and lower cities, and access is controlled by Palladian security at every transition point. Workers descend in the morning and ascend in the evening, their movements tracked, their productivity monitored, their bodies gradually absorbing the particulate matter that the filtration systems don't quite catch. The lower city's air quality is rated 'acceptable' by corporate standards, which means it will kill you slowly rather than quickly.

Burlington Bay has been converted into a shipping hub for metallurgical products, connected to the broader Lake Ontario cargo network by automated barge lines. The waterfront is industrial infrastructure — cranes, smelters, cargo handling systems — with no concession to aesthetics or public access. The old Bayfront Park is now a materials staging area. The residential neighborhoods south and east of the escarpment maintain a grim vitality — these are communities that have survived a century of industrial exploitation by developing an immunity to corporate promises and a talent for mutual aid. Steelmouth's people are hard, practical, and deeply skeptical of anyone who arrives with a plan for their improvement.

sights: The escarpment face lit by cargo elevator lights at shift change — a vertical river of workers ascending
Foundry glow reflecting off Burlington Bay at night, turning the water copper and orange
Smoke stacks and processing towers rising above the lower city like a forest of industrial trees
Palladian security checkpoints at every escarpment elevator — scanners, ID verification, the daily ritual of proving you belong
The upper city's residential towers, clean and modern, looking down on the source of their wealth
sounds: The foundries — a deep, rhythmic pounding that the lower city's residents feel in their bones
Cargo cranes on the bay, hydraulic and relentless, loading barges around the clock
Shift-change sirens — the city's actual clock, more reliable than anything digital
Wind off the escarpment carrying industrial particulate — you hear it hit the filtration masks before you feel it
smells: Hot metal — the dominant note, always, everywhere in the lower city
Ozone from the electric arc furnaces, sharp and persistent
Burlington Bay water, mineral-heavy and warm from industrial discharge
The upper city smells like nothing, which is the most expensive smell there is
atmosphere.feel: A city divided vertically by geology and horizontally by class. Steelmouth doesn't pretend. The escarpment makes the hierarchy visible, literal, carved into the landscape. Everyone knows their elevation, and everyone knows what it means.

demographics: Population 1.8 million. The lower city is 70% Tier 1 and Tier 2 manufacturing workers. The upper city is Tier 3 and 4 corporate employees. The excluded live in the escarpment tunnels — old mine shafts and drainage channels converted into informal housing. Nobody counts them.
economy: Advanced metallurgy and construction materials. Steelmouth produces 30% of the augmentation-grade alloys used in the eastern GLMZ and 60% of the structural composites for arcology construction. The economy is monoculture — when the foundries slow, everything slows. Palladian and Ashgrave set the pace, and the city walks to it.
power_structure: Palladian Construction holds the largest sovereign enclave. Ashgrave Materials holds the second. Between them they employ 65% of the working population. The municipal government administers the upper city residential zones and maintains the polite fiction that it governs the whole. The lower city's informal labor council has more practical authority than the mayor.
dangers: Industrial accidents — the foundries are dangerous, the safety standards are 'adequate,' and the distinction kills people
Escarpment access control — get your credentials revoked and you're trapped in the lower city
Particulate exposure — the long-term health effects are documented, ignored, and fatal
Labor disputes that turn physical — Steelmouth's workers have a history of direct action
Escarpment tunnel collapses in the informal housing zones
opportunities: Metallurgical expertise is rare and valuable — skilled workers can name their price outside Steelmouth
The labor council needs operatives for contract disputes that can't be resolved through negotiation
Ashgrave and Palladian sabotage each other constantly — there's always work for someone willing to get their hands dirty
The escarpment tunnels connect to pre-corporate infrastructure that nobody has fully mapped
story_hooks: A new alloy being produced in the Palladian foundries has properties that don't match any known metallurgical process — and the engineers who developed it have stopped showing up to work
The escarpment tunnel network connects to something beneath the bay that predates the foundries by centuries — and Ashgrave is quietly excavating it
Steelmouth's labor council is organizing a cross-corporate strike that would shut down augmentation-grade alloy production across the eastern GLMZ
